title: BlackRock Just Turned Neutral On U.S. Stocks. It Hasn't Given Up On AI. - The Wealth Advisor
text: BlackRock has ended its longstanding overweight position in U.S. equities, downgrading stocks to neutral while upgrading Treasurys for the first time in years. The world's largest asset manager isn't predicting a market collapse or abandoning the artificial intelligence boom. Its strategists have decided that bond yields have risen enough to make taking profits in stocks more attractive than continuing to carry the same exposure to market risk. The shift, announced Monday by BlackRock Investment Institute strategists Jean Boivin, Rick Rieder and Wei Li, reverses a Treasury underweight that had been a fixture of the firm's positioning for most of the past six years. Short-term U.S. Treasurys move to overweight, while longer-term government bonds rise to neutral. BlackRock is financing those changes by reducing its U.S. equity allocation, a meaningful decision from an institution that has remained constructive on American stocks through much of the AI-driven rally. The immediate attraction is income. Treasury yields have climbed sharply as investors reassess inflation, federal borrowing and the likelihood that the Federal Reserve will need to raise rates again. BlackRock believes markets may have become too aggressive in anticipating additional tightening, creating an opportunity to lock in higher yields without accepting the same risks embedded in equity valuations. That doesn't mean the firm suddenly expects interest rates to collapse. Rieder and his colleagues see enough compensation in short-term government securities to justify owning more of them, while remaining more measured about longer maturities. The distinction matters after a prolonged bond selloff in which investors have repeatedly discovered that attractive yields don't necessarily protect against further price declines. The more interesting part of BlackRock's decision is what it says about stocks. Its strategists continue to believe in the earnings potential of artificial intelligence, but they also see greater volatility surrounding the extraordinary capital expenditures required to build the technology. The firm is preserving its preference for AI-related companies within U.S. equities even as it reduces its conviction in the broader market. That is a narrower retreat than the headline downgrade might suggest. BlackRock isn't arguing that Nvidia, Microsoft and the other beneficiaries of AI investment have suddenly lost their economic advantages. It is questioning whether the market's willingness to reward the entire investment cycle can remain as dependable when financing costs are rising and investors are beginning to scrutinize the returns on enormous infrastructure commitments. The distinction has become increasingly visible beneath the major indexes. According to figures from the Kobeissi Letter cited in Tuesday's market reporting, 84% of S&P 500 constituents are trading at least 10% below their all-time highs, while 59% are down at least 20%. A market that remains relatively close to its records can therefore conceal substantial weakness among companies without the earnings momentum or investor enthusiasm enjoyed by the largest technology businesses. Higher Treasury yields are helping produce that divide. Companies with strong cash generation and exceptional growth can continue attracting capital even when borrowing becomes more expensive. Businesses dependent on refinancing, consumer spending or more modest earnings growth face a less forgiving environment. The AI trade has helped sustain the indexes, but it hasn't insulated the rest of corporate America from the consequences of tighter financial conditions. BlackRock's decision also reflects a change in the competition for investment capital. When Treasury yields were exceptionally low, investors had relatively little incentive to surrender equity upside for government-bond income. With yields substantially higher, that calculation becomes less automatic. Stocks must offer enough prospective return to justify their volatility against an alternative that now pays investors meaningfully to wait. There is a limit to how far BlackRock is willing to take that argument. Its strategists aren't moving aggressively into long-duration Treasurys, where persistent inflation and fiscal concerns could continue pushing yields higher. Nor are they abandoning equities in favor of a wholesale defensive allocation. They are reducing an established preference for stocks because the relative opportunities have changed. That makes the timing significant. BlackRock has spent years benefiting from an investment environment in which American equities, particularly the largest technology companies, repeatedly justified optimism. Now the same firm sees enough uncertainty around AI spending and enough opportunity in fixed income to stop pressing that advantage. The AI revolution may still deliver the earnings growth its champions expect. BlackRock simply no longer believes investors need to make quite as large a bet on the stock market while waiting for that future to arrive.
